new_statements.translation: Each word is characterized by a primary accent, phonemic as the following minimal pairs attest: /'akoro/ 'with you', /a'koro/ 'with him' [...]. Two-syllable words generally take the primary or strong accent on the last syllable, e.g. /to'ho/ 'heart', /ka'mi/ 'blood' [...]. We find exceptions in /'kwama/ 'house', /'papa/ 'father (voc.)' when they occur in isolation; once inside a pause group they take the primary accent on the last syllable. In words of 4 or more syllables there may be a non-phonemic secondary accent. In the specific case of 4-syllable words it appears on the 4th syllable, while the primary accent is on the 2nd syllable, e.g. [ta'rako'ro] 'all' [...]. Five-syllable words take the accents on the 2nd and 5th syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word accent falls on the second syllable of the phonological word: disyllables are final-stressed (= 2nd), all trisyllabic examples given are marked on the 2nd syllable (/a'sakre/, /ka'yahi/, /tak'pire/, /ka'myere/), 4-syllable words have primary on the 2nd with a secondary on the 4th; 5-syllable words carry accents on the 2nd and 5th (the wording 'secundário e primário' suggests primary on the 5th there). The author nonetheless labels the primary accent phonemic on the strength of one prefixal minimal pair (/'akoro/ 2nd person vs /a'koro/ 3rd person) and a few initial-stressed disyllables in isolation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-phonemic secondary accent in words of 4+ syllables: on the 4th syllable in 4-syllable words ([ta'rako'ro], [ku'rata'ku]); in 5-syllable words accents on 2nd and 5th with two syllables between secondary and primary ([a'marisi'pa] 'tamanduá-bandeira', [a'kayahi'ni] 'your axe').
new_statements.exceptions: /'kwama/ 'house' and /'papa/ 'father (vocative)' are initial-stressed in isolation but final-stressed inside a pause group; minimal pair /'akoro/ 'with you' vs /a'koro/ 'with him' (and plural /'akoro?ne/ vs /a'koro?ne/) cited as evidence that primary accent is phonemic. Footnote 16: pitch generally changes where tonic accent occurs, though the author will not affirm that word/pause-group pitch depends on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'palavra fonológica' (which the author notes does not always coincide with the morphological word); isolation forms vs pause-group forms differ for the exceptional disyllables. Separately (p.18) the intonation group carries a strong phrase accent 'geralmente na última sílaba ou na penúltima'.
new_statements.identity_note: Wallace 1970 describes the speech of the Kaxuyâna group relocated from the Rio Cachorro/Trombetas (Pará) to the Tiriyó mission area (Paru de Oeste); data collected 1968 with Museu Nacional standard wordlist. Same language as Glottolog kaxu1237 (Kaxuiâna, ISO kbb); no separate dialect glottocode. The author (Ruth Wallace de Garcia Paula) published under 'Wallace, R.' in 1970 and 'Paula, R.W.G.' later.

new_statements.translation: Each word is characterized by primary stress, which is phonemic as the following minimal pairs attest: /'akoro/ 'with you (sg.)', /a'koro/ 'with him', /'akoro?ne/ 'with you (pl.)', /a'koro?ne/ 'with them'. Two-syllable words generally receive primary (strong) stress on the last syllable, e.g. /to'ho/ 'heart', /ka'mi/ 'blood', /a'koy/ 'snake'. We find exceptions in /'kwama/ 'house', /'papa/ 'father (vocative)' when they occur in isolation. [...] In four-syllable words the (non-phonemic) secondary stress falls on the 4th syllable while primary stress is on the 2nd syllable, e.g. [ta'rako'ro] 'all'. (The stress mark precedes the stressed syllable, per her footnote 8.)

new_statements.reading: Wallace codes Kaxuyâna word stress as phonemic (contrastive) on the strength of the akoro pairs, but with strong default patterns: disyllables are final-stressed (with a few initial-stressed exceptions in isolation that become final-stressed inside a pause group); 4-syllable words have primary stress on the 2nd syllable and secondary on the 4th; 5-syllable words carry stresses on the 2nd and 5th syllables (she does not say unambiguously which is primary; by analogy to the 4-syllable case the 2nd is primary). Net: a left-edge-anchored primary (2nd syllable) in longer words with a right-edge secondary, i.e. a rhythmic/alternating system in the Cariban mould, finality in disyllables, and lexical contrast asserted. She adds (p. 18) that the intonation group carries a strong phrasal accent usually on the last or penultimate syllable. This is the only first-hand phonological description of Kaxuyâna found online; Paula 1977/1980 (the fuller phonology, Publ. Avulsas Museu Nacional 63) and Derbyshire 1961 are not online (checked Museu Goeldi DSpace, BDTD, Crossref, archive.org).
